title: Hospitals Are Deploying AI Faster Than Regulators Can Keep Up, Landmark Review Warns
source_used: Scienmag (original of the Bioengineer.org copy); abstract checked at Frontiers
key_facts: A systematic review and regulatory gap analysis in Frontiers in Digital Health, led by Joseph Conteh of the University of New Mexico with Naim Kapucu, Eunice F. Ebevuhe and Oluwapelumi Wumi Adeniji, examines AI governance in US hospitals.
By the end of 2025 the FDA had authorised more than 1,451 AI and machine-learning-enabled medical devices.
Of 1,065 records identified, 22 studies met the criteria; the review found four critical gaps: post-market monitoring, equity assurance, accountability clarification and governance capacity.
A COVID-19 chest X-ray AI tool that scored above 0.95 on open datasets dropped to about 0.70 after deployment in hospitals.

Only 58.1% of hospitals in a national sample did post-implementation monitoring in 2024, and 79% of hospitals use predictive models created by electronic health record vendors with no framework for sharing accountability.
The authors propose a six-part lifecycle governance framework and compare the US patchwork of FDA, ONC and CMS authority with the EU AI Act.

Limitations: retrospective protocol registration, English-language studies only, four databases, and much of the evidence is retrospective and single-centre; the CMS quality link is observational, not causal.
The Frontiers record gives the publication date as 14 Oct 2026.
quote_evidence: Yet according to a new systematic review and regulatory gap analysis published in Frontiers in Digital Health, the governance frameworks meant to keep patients safe have not kept pace with this explosive deployment—and the consequences are already measurable.
Of 1,065 records identified, just 22 studies met the eligibility criteria.
The structured gap analysis identified four critical, structurally interconnected failures.
why_it_matters_hint: Hospital AI is spreading faster than the rules that check it keeps working and treats all patients fairly.
event_date: Study published 14 Oct 2026 (Frontiers record); Scienmag report 16 Oct 2026.
